why/slip: Backprop works out a gradient by rules, one local slope at a time, and a single slip makes it wrong. Take f as x squared: its slope is two x, so six at x equals three.
why/wrong: Write x where two x belongs, and backprop says three. Its line there is too flat, yet nothing crashes, and nothing warns you.
why/bottou: Léon Bottou described this trap in 2012. A program stepping downhill along a slightly wrong gradient still runs, but often slowly and erratically, and such bugs can sit in code used quietly for years.
why/measure: Reading the code line by line, he wrote, is the wrong way to check. Instead, measure the slope straight from f: nudge x, and watch f move.
why/cost: That is the slow way, one more run of f for every input: too slow to use every time, but fine for a check.
numeric/sides: Step a small distance h to each side of three, here a tenth. There, f is nine point six one on the right, and eight point four one on the left.
numeric/divide: Rise over run: their difference, one point two, over the distance between them, two h, since each point sits h from three. That gives six.
numeric/name: This is the centered difference, centered because its two points sit evenly around x. A difference over a real, finite step, instead of the limit, is called a finite difference.
numeric/caught: It says six, and backprop said three. They disagree, so backprop has a bug.
numeric/one: Why two points? A one-sided step, from three to three point one, gives six point one: a tenth too high. The centered one is exactly right here.
error/cube: That exactness belongs to x squared. Take x cubed at one, where the power rule gives the slope: three x squared, so three.
error/one: With h a tenth, the one-sided secant, from one to one point one, has slope three point three one: off by zero point three one.
error/mid: The centered secant, from zero point nine to one point one, has slope three point zero one: off by only zero point zero one, though its points are twice as far apart.
error/left: Why? Step to the left instead, from zero point nine to one. That slope is two point seven one: too low by zero point two nine, about as much as the right step was too high.
error/cancel: The centered slope is the average of the two, three point zero one. One overshoots, the other undershoots, and their errors nearly cancel.
error/shrink: Now shrink h ten times, to a hundredth. The one-sided error shrinks about ten times too, to about three hundredths.
error/shrink2: The centered error shrinks a hundred times, to one ten-thousandth.
error/order: So the one-sided error shrinks like h, and the centered error like h squared: a tenth of the step, a hundredth of the error.
compare/a: Call backprop's answer A, the analytic gradient: worked out from formulas.
compare/n: Call the measured one n, the numerical gradient: measured from the values of f.
compare/gap: Their gap alone says too little. Off by one ten-thousandth is nothing next to a thousand, but huge next to two ten-thousandths.
compare/abs: So take the gap as a size: the absolute value of A minus n. The bars mean absolute value, a number with its sign dropped.
compare/rel: Then divide it by the larger of the two sizes. That is the relative error: the gap as a fraction of the numbers being compared.
compare/ok: As a rule of thumb, a relative error of ten to the minus seven, one ten-millionth, or less, means the two agree: backprop is right.
compare/sus: Near ten to the minus four, one ten-thousandth, be suspicious: it is worth a closer look.
compare/bug: At ten to the minus two, one hundredth, or more, there is a bug.
compare/ex: The slip from before gave three where the slope is six: a gap of three, over the larger size, six. A relative error of a half: clearly a bug.
